config.prompt: Kingdon's multiple streams — pair each with what flows in it:

pairs.right: designs waiting in departments, think tanks and academia

config.why: When all three align — a crisis makes a problem visible, a ready plan exists, the politics permits it — a window opens briefly and major change happens fast.

activities.anchor: Two British cases show the mechanism
activities.caption: scrub the two windows that became law
activities.name: ppCasesTimeline

events.title: The Great Smog
events.text: thousands dead in London (later analyses put the toll around 12,000) — coal smoke the obvious cause

events.title: The Clean Air Act
events.text: within four years of the smog — after a decade in which smoke abatement bills had repeatedly failed

events.title: The Dunblane shooting
events.text: sixteen children and a teacher killed in March 1996

events.title: The handgun ban
events.text: legislation that had been stuck for years passes within a year

activities.caption: bet on what coverage alone buys
activities.name: ppMediaPredict

config.q: A scandal dominates the front pages for weeks. Does the coverage itself cause policy?
choices: yes — attention is the whole mechanism
no — a window still needs a workable solution and political willingness
config.why: Scandals that had neither — countless inquiries 'accepted in full' and then quietly shelved — show all three streams are required.

activities.caption: file each adoption feature under its system
activities.name: ppVetoSort

config.prompt: Two adoption machineries — file each feature:

items.label: a government with a Commons majority can normally pass its programme
the unelected second chamber can only delay (Parliament Acts 1911, 1949)
no separate elected president to veto anything
a Supreme Court willing to strike laws down

config.why: Concentration is double-edged: fast enough to pass the poll tax quickly — and fast enough that its design flaws could not be stopped.

activities.anchor: Behind the cycle sits a fight about rationality
activities.caption: one line of this decision-models briefing is wrong
activities.name: ppRationalSpot

config.prompt: One line of this student's briefing on decision models is wrong — click it:
lines: The rational-comprehensive model says decision-makers should define goals, list every option, cost each, and choose the optimum.
Herbert Simon showed humans have bounded rationality — limited time, information and attention — so they satisfice.
Lindblom's incrementalism: real policy advances by small adjustments to what exists, negotiated between partisans.
The garbage-can model is the anarchic limit case: solutions, problems and decision-makers float independently and collide by chance.
Real governments optimise in practice — the models only correct the textbooks.
config.correction: Governments should be rational but are in fact incremental — the policy windows are the moments when the incremental fog briefly lifts.
config.why: Big radical designs outrun anyone's ability to predict their effects, which is why muddling through is the observed behaviour.

activities.anchor: Its powers come in three flavours
activities.caption: true or false — the prerogative and its policing
activities.name: ppPrerogJudge

statements.s: The royal prerogative still lets ministers declare war, sign treaties and appoint ministers without a vote.
statements.why: The residue of medieval monarchical power, exercised by ministers.

statements.s: The prerogative is the monarch's personal power, exercised from the throne.
statements.why: It is ministerial power wearing historical dress — the Crown reigns; the prerogative governs.

statements.s: Miller II (2019) ruled the five-week prorogation of Parliament unlawful — prerogative power is reviewable.
statements.why: A unanimous verdict that its use is reviewable like any other executive act.

statements.s: The 2011 Fixed-term Parliaments Act clawed back election-timing discretion — and was itself repealed in 2022.
statements.why: Parliament has clawed some prerogative back; the courts police the rest.

activities.anchor: Is Britain governed by the Cabinet
activities.caption: drag the divider — the PM's standing moves the centre
activities.name: ppPMCompare

config.prompt: Drag the divider — prime-ministerial command versus the parliamentary core:

before.label: commanding the party
before.text: Thatcher early, Blair with big majorities: sofa government decided in informal bilaterals, and the Iraq War decision (2003) taken with a tiny circle though formally endorsed.

after.label: losing the party
after.text: Thatcher by the end: cabinet resignation is the exit-interview logic — the system's parliamentary core reasserts itself.

config.why: Neither pure cabinet government nor a presidency: a parliament-centred system whose centre of gravity moves with one politician's standing.

activities.anchor: Two conventions tie the executive to Parliament
activities.caption: file each case under its convention
activities.name: ppResponsibilitySort

config.prompt: The accountability conventions — file each case and rule:

items.label: a minister answers for the personal conduct and failings of their department
Crichel Down 1954: Dugdale resigned although officials had mismanaged the land deal
Amber Rudd's resignation in April 2018 over the Windrush deportations
Cabinet decisions bind all ministers, who must defend them publicly or resign
Robin Cook's resignation over the Iraq War (2003)
suspended for the 2016 EU referendum — ministers campaigned on opposite sides

config.why: Conventions, not laws: Priti Patel breached the Ministerial Code in 2020 and kept her job with the PM's backing — which is why critics want the code's adviser independent of the PM.
